prime.problem: TCP checksums, link CRCs and retransmits all "guarantee" delivery, yet files still arrive corrupted: bytes get damaged while sitting in a router's memory between two checks, or the receiving app crashes after the kernel ACKed. If only the applications at the two ends know whether the job was done right, no lower layer can promise it for them.
prime.fits: Builds on the unreliable-network card: silence and damage happen. This card says where the correctness check must live (at the ends) and what lower layers are for (making that check fail less often). It reappears in idempotency keys and the exactly-once transfer.
expect: careful file transfer and the MIT gateway
FIN/RST crash signals vs a 20 s timeout
prime.goal: Explain why correctness checks belong at the endpoints, compute what chunk size keeps resends cheap, and write a TCP exchange where the sender knows the receiving app got every byte.

attend: Every link CRC passed in the simulation, yet the file was wrong. Where exactly was the damage introduced?
Why does a 10 GB file at 10<sup>−9</sup> per byte per hop over 10 hops essentially never get through whole, and what fixes that?
What does sendall() returning tell A, and what does it not tell A?
Why does half-closing with shutdown(SHUT_WR) let A wait for B's own answer?
Why is a FIN from a killed process a far faster failure signal than a ZooKeeper session timeout, and when can you not rely on it?

must: Only the endpoints can see every fault on the path (router memory, disk, a crash after the ACK) → the correctness check must be end to end → lower-layer checks can't make the result correct, only make the end check fail less often (a performance choice)

Undetected damage per byte per hop p → expected bad bytes S·h·p → P(one clean try) ≈ e<sup>−Shp</sup> → at λ = 100 (10 GB, 10 hops, 10<sup>−9</sup>) whole-file retries never finish → hash and resend per chunk: 1 MB chunks cost 1.0% extra
sendall()/close() return once A's kernel has the bytes → say nothing about B's app → half-close, let B hash everything it read and send the digest back → A compares: an application-level ACK
The OS outlives a crashed process → it sends FIN/RST at once (0.3–1.2 ms on localhost) → far faster than a 20 s session timeout → use crash signals to cut MTTR, keep the timeout for real partitions
elevated: Expected sends per chunk = 1 / P(clean) = e<sup>λ</sup> → cost grows exponentially with chunk size → halving λ near 1 matters a lot, far below 1 hardly at all (10 MB: 10.5%, 1 MB: 1.0%)
reference: the Python socket calls' exact signatures
Saltzer, Reed and Clark 1984 section numbers
the simulation's seeded byte counts (1,065,536 and 9,000,000 bytes sent)

compress.prompt: In three sentences from memory: where the correctness check lives and why, what lower-layer reliability is for, and how the half-close gives A an application-level answer. Then write the chunk-size formula.
checklist: only the endpoints can check the whole path, so the check is end to end
lower-layer checks are a performance optimisation, not a guarantee
whole-file retry cost explodes as e<sup>Shp</sup>; chunk it
kernel-level success (sendall, close, TCP ACK) ≠ the app got it
half-close + digest reply = the app's own acknowledgement
crash signals (FIN/RST) cut detection time; timeouts remain for partitions

retrieve.q: Explain the end-to-end argument using the MIT gateway story: why didn't per-hop checksums catch the corruption?
answer: each hop's checksum covered only its own wire
the gateway swapped bytes while copying between buffers, after one check and before the next
only a check computed by the sender's app and verified by the receiver's app covers that gap

retrieve.q: Walk through the seven steps of the Python half-close exchange: who sends what, and at which step does A finally know B's app has every byte?
answer: B reads until recv() returns b"", hashing as it goes
B sends the sha256 digest, then closes (its FIN)
A reads the 32 bytes until b"" and compares with its own hash: only at step 7 does A know

retrieve.q: Your network team offers to make every hop 100× more reliable (p = 10<sup>−11</sup>). With whole-file transfers of 10 GB, is that a better investment than 1 MB chunking? Use the card's numbers.
answer: at 10<sup>−11</sup>, λ = 1: P(clean) = 0.368, 2.72 tries per file, so 172% extra bytes
1 MB chunking at the original 10<sup>−9</sup> costs 1.0% extra
chunking wins by far; better hops are only worth it where they're cheap, and the end check stays either way

compare.q: An idempotency key and a file digest are both end-to-end mechanisms. What does each check, who chooses the value, and what does each fail to cover on its own?
answer: the digest checks the content arrived unchanged; the sender's app computes it from the data
the key checks a request wasn't applied twice; the client picks it once per operation
a key only dedupes one hop, so the service behind needs its own; a digest says nothing about duplicates

compare.q: The registry detects dead servers with a 20 s session timeout; this card detects a killed process in about a millisecond. Why doesn't ZooKeeper just use FIN, and how do the two combine?
answer: FIN only comes if the OS survives: a machine that loses power or a partition sends nothing
a GC-paused process sends nothing either, so it still needs the timeout
combine: act on crash signals immediately (HBase's admin kill), and keep the timeout for silent failures

predict.q: A path has 5 hops (not 10), still 10<sup>−9</sup> per byte per hop, and you hash in 100 MB chunks. What percentage of extra bytes do you expect to resend, and is that closer to the card's 100 MB row or its 10 MB row? Commit first.
predict.answer: λ = 10<sup>8</sup> × 5 × 10<sup>−9</sup> = 0.5, so extra = e<sup>0.5</sup> − 1 = 64.9%. It sits between the card's 100 MB row (λ = 1, 172%) and 10 MB row (λ = 0.1, 10.5%). Halving the hops halves λ, but because the cost is exponential in λ, you'd still want smaller chunks: 10 MB at 5 hops is λ = 0.05, about 5.1%.

apply.task: Extend send_file/receiver from code/end-to-end-argument.py to send a file in 64 KB chunks, each followed by B's digest reply for that chunk; A resends any chunk whose digest doesn't match. Inject corruption on B's side (flip a byte with probability 10−6 per byte, seeded) and count resends for a 1 MB file. Compare your count with the expected eλ − 1 per chunk.
apply.done: Every chunk's digest matches after at most a few resends, the file on B's side equals A's, and your measured extra bytes are in the same ballpark as the formula: λ per chunk = 65,536 × 10<sup>−6</sup> ≈ 0.066, so about 6.8% extra, noisy for only 16 chunks.
apply.hint: e<sup>0.0655</sup> − 1 = 0.0677. With 16 chunks you expect about one resend in total; run several seeds before trusting the average.
